open-question.question: The mission's goal opens with a hands-on check of what Claude Desktop accepts from outside (a prompt, a folder, a model, an effort, a permission mode), and most of the feature's design hinges on what that check finds. Is the check run before the mission's remaining open questions are answered, with its findings written into the relevant starting state, or as the mission's first task after task derivation, with the decisions made beforehand written to hold for whichever outcome it finds?
open-question.alternative: The whole hands-on check (the `claude://code/new` link and the `claude --desktop` option, each tried for a prefilled or already-sent prompt, the folder the session opens on, and any model, effort, or permission mode it takes) is run now, by the person at the machine, outside any task, before the recommendation pass and the answer sweep run over the mission's questions; its findings are written into `## Relevant starting state` beside the static reading of Claude Desktop 5.11492.5 already there, and every open question is then recommended and answered against observed behaviour. If no prompt can be passed, the mission stops at that point, before any decision is recorded. Every decision that hinges on Desktop's behaviour (which opening mechanism, what happens to uncarried values, the over-long prompt, the stop conditions) is made against what Desktop was seen to do rather than against a guess, so no decision has to be written conditionally and the stop, if it comes, costs no decision work at all. The check is work outside the workflow's steps: no skill runs it, and since `specify-mission-starting-state` explores again only when `since` prints commits past its anchor, the findings reach the section by a hand edit or through a commit of the check's record that moves the ground (where that record lives is the sibling question on the check's record); the whole preparation waits until a person sits down with Claude Desktop, and picks formed before the findings land would need stripping.

The full hands-on check runs before answering, as in a pre-answer check with its findings written into `## Relevant starting state`, but only the questions whose answer hinges on its outcome wait for it; the questions that hold whatever it finds (how Desktop is selected for an action, the Harnesses row, the listing texts, the send feedback) are recommended and answered now, each through a single-question answer skill rather than the whole-mission sweep. Preparation keeps moving on the outcome-independent questions while the check waits for a person at the machine, and the decisions that do hinge on Desktop are still made against observed behaviour. Sorting the questions into dependent and independent is a judgment that can miss a dependency (a selection mechanism may yet hinge on whether Desktop takes a folder), the answer sweep cannot be used while some picks must be held, and a stop after the check leaves the independent decisions already recorded as wasted work.

Only the part of the check that decides whether the mission goes on and which mechanism can carry a prompt (does a prompt arrive through the link and through `claude --desktop`, prefilled or sent, and on which folder) is run now and written into `## Relevant starting state` before answering; the rest (whether `claude --desktop` takes a model, an effort, or a permission mode, how a long prompt behaves in practice) is the mission's first task after task derivation, with the decisions it touches written to hold for either outcome. The stop condition and the facts most decisions turn on are settled before any decision is made, at the cost of a short check, while the details whose outcome only shapes what the feature carries stay inside the task pipeline with a verified bar of their own. The line between the two parts is drawn before anyone has seen Desktop, so a fact left to the task may prove to decide a question already answered, and the decisions over the deferred part must still be written conditionally; the pre-answer part shares the hand-edit route into the starting state of a full pre-answer check.

The full hands-on check runs before answering, its findings written into `## Relevant starting state` and every question answered against them, and task derivation also places a first task that repeats the check against the Claude Desktop version installed when execution starts, stopping the run where the findings no longer hold. Decisions are made against observed behaviour, and the feature is still built against the behaviour that holds when it is built, which matters for an application updated as often as Claude Desktop (its static reading names a build number, 5.11492.5, not a stable interface). The check is run twice, the second time by a task that needs a person to watch Desktop (an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run cannot see whether a prompt arrived prefilled), and a changed finding at that point means revising recorded decisions after task derivation, which the workflow has no step for beyond revert and re-answer.

No check runs before answering: every open question is recommended and answered now against the static reading in `## Relevant starting state`, each decision that hinges on Desktop's behaviour written to hold for whichever outcome the check finds (a conditional pick of mechanism, values, and stop), and the hands-on check is the mission's first task after task derivation, its outcome choosing among the prepared branches and, where no prompt can be passed, stopping the mission there. The check runs inside the workflow, as a task with a derived and verified acceptance bar recorded in its `Task-completion:` commit, and preparation proceeds at once through the ordinary review, annotation, and answer sweep with no hand edit of the starting state. Conditional decisions are harder to write and to derive tasks from, every branch the check does not take is decision work spent for nothing, a stop after derivation leaves a task list holding feature tasks that must be removed before `finish-mission` will run, and the task needs a person to observe Desktop, so it cannot run in an unattended `complete-all-tasks` pass; how far the stop reaches depends on the sibling question on the check's stop conditions.

open-question.question: The goal stops the mission when the hands-on check finds that no prompt can be passed to Claude Desktop. Which other findings, if any, stop it the same way: a session that cannot be opened on the project's folder, a Desktop session in which the Gurita plugin's `/gurita:` skills are not available, or none?
open-question.alternative: No stop list beyond the goal's is fixed now. The check runs, and a finding that the session cannot be opened on the project's folder or that the `/gurita:` skills are not available is weighed when it is found, as a goal revision or a new open question, deciding then whether the mission stops, narrows, or goes on with a hand step. The decision is made against what Desktop actually does rather than against guesses, since nothing about how a folder or the plugin reaches a Desktop session has been observed, and a finding nobody foresaw (the session opening but reading another plugin copy, for instance) gets the same treatment as the two named ones. It leaves the mission's end condition open, so the decisions taken before the check cannot be written to hold for every outcome, and it works only where the check's findings reach a point at which a question can still be asked; whether they do is the hands-on check timing question's, and run as a task after derivation the check leaves no such point without stopping the task run.

No finding beyond the goal's own stops the mission. A session that cannot be opened on the project's folder does not stop it, and the feature opens the Desktop session wherever Desktop puts it, leaving the person to move it to the project's folder. A Desktop session without the `/gurita:` skills does not stop it either, and the feature sends the prompt as the line carries it, leaving the person to make the plugin available in Desktop. The stop list stays exactly the goal's: no prompt can be passed. It keeps the goal as written and lets the mission ship whatever the check finds short of the one stated failure, so a partial result (the prompt arrives but the folder or the skills need a hand step) still gives the person Desktop's visual and sound artifacts, which is the reason the harness exists. The feature can ship as a button that opens a session where the skill invocation in its prompt does nothing, or one working on the wrong folder, so the action the person clicked is not the action that runs. What the person is told about that hand step falls to the questions on the Desktop Harnesses row, send feedback, and harness availability, and the feature is only as usable as those answers make it.

Two findings stop the mission: no prompt can be passed, or no session can be opened on the project's folder (neither the `claude://code/new` link's `folder` parameter nor the `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option puts the session there). A Desktop session without the `/gurita:` skills does not stop it, and the feature sends the prompt as the line carries it, leaving the person to make the plugin available in Desktop. Every Gurita action reads and writes a mission inside the project, so a session on another folder cannot do the work at all and is likely to write into the wrong tree, while missing skills are a one-time setup step the person can fix in Desktop and then rely on. It ships a feature whose prompts invoke skills Desktop may not have, so a fresh Desktop install sends a `/gurita:` prompt that resolves to nothing until the person installs the plugin there, with nothing in the extension's checks today able to tell (every Harnesses check assumes a CLI). Whether that gap is shown falls to the Desktop Harnesses row question.

Two findings stop the mission: no prompt can be passed, or the `/gurita:` skills are not available in the Desktop session opened (Desktop does not load the Gurita plugin copy Claude Code has, and offers no way to install it). A session that cannot be opened on the project's folder does not stop it, and the feature opens the session wherever Desktop puts it, leaving the person to pick the project's folder in Desktop. Every action the harness serves is a `/gurita:` skill invocation, so without the skills the prompt is plain text and the feature does nothing Gurita-specific, while a folder the person picks once in Desktop's own picker is a small hand step that leaves the action intact. It ships a feature that can open the session on a folder other than the project's, so until the person moves it the skill runs against the wrong tree or finds no mission, and a person who misses the step gets a session that writes outside the project. Whether the folder can be reached at all from a remote window is the harness availability question's, and this option leaves that case to it.

Three findings stop the mission the same way: no prompt can be passed, no session can be opened on the project's folder, or the `/gurita:` skills are not available in the Desktop session. The feature is built only when the check finds a session that opens on the project's folder, with the prompt prefilled, and with the skills it invokes available; otherwise the mission stops at the check and records why. The feature ships only when a click does what the action promises, the named skill running on the project's mission, so no button opens a session that silently cannot do its job and no hand step has to be documented or detected. It is the strictest bar and the likeliest to end the mission with nothing built, even where a hand step (picking the folder once, installing the plugin in Desktop once) would have made the feature work, which gives up the visual and sound artifacts the goal is after for a gap the person could close themselves.

open-question.question: When an action is sent to Claude Desktop and Desktop takes no model, effort, or permission mode from outside, what becomes of the `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass-permission values the action's line carries: are they dropped without sign, or is the person shown, in the Settings window or on the action's button, that the Desktop session will not carry them?
open-question.alternative: The premise that the line goes on carrying values Desktop does not take is rejected: when a line is set to go to Claude Desktop, the stored line is rewritten without whichever of `--model`, `--effort`, and the bypass flag Desktop does not take, so nothing is uncarried and no indicator is needed; what the line text shows is what the session gets. The line is truthful by construction, so the Settings window's line editor already shows exactly what the Desktop session carries, with no separate indicator to build or keep in step. Switching the line back to a terminal harness loses the values the person had set, and the rewrite applies only if Desktop is selected by rewriting a line, which the Desktop selection mechanism sibling question owns; a shipped variant sent to Desktop without a rewrite would still drop its values without sign.

The line keeps its `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass flag as written, and on a send to Claude Desktop whichever of them Desktop does not take (as the hands-on check finds) is dropped with no sign anywhere in the extension's windows or buttons; `gurita-vscode/USAGE.md` states once, where it documents the Desktop harness, that a Desktop session runs on Desktop's own model, effort, and permission mode and which line values it does not carry. Adds no UI, no state, and no test beyond the send itself, keeping the fire-and-forget feature as small as the goal frames it, and the values stay on the line unchanged for when the same variant is run in a terminal again. A person who picked a variant for its model or effort, or for its bypass flag, gets a session that silently differs: every shipped single-interactive-line variant carries `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--model`, and `--effort`, so an `Execute tasks` sent to Desktop runs `complete-all-tasks` under Desktop's permission prompts and its default model with nothing in VS Code saying so.

The line keeps its values; where the Settings window lets a person select Claude Desktop for an action's line, that line (or its variant) is marked with the values it carries that Desktop does not take, named as they stand on the line (for example the model, the effort, and the bypass flag), only those the hands-on check finds uncarried; the action's button and the send show nothing. Tells the person at the one moment a deliberate choice is made, with the exact values, and adds no clutter to the mission pages' buttons, which keep their current look. Reaches only someone who opens the Settings window: a Desktop selection made earlier, or a shipped variant used from a button, still sends without sign at the click; where the mark can sit depends on the selection mechanism a sibling question owns.

The line keeps its values; whenever an action's selected variant goes to Claude Desktop, its button in the page (its label, variant dropdown entry, or hover text) shows that the Desktop session will not carry the line's model, effort, or bypass values, naming those the hands-on check finds uncarried; the Settings window shows nothing of it. Tells the person right where and when they are about to send, every time, including for a selection made long before or remembered in `workspaceState`. Adds wording to buttons that today carry none of their lines' details, across the six button sites in `src/pane.ts` and `src/finishedWindow.ts`, and gives no sign at the moment the Desktop selection is made in Settings.

The line keeps its values; both the Settings window, where Desktop is selected for the line, and the action's button, while its selected variant goes to Desktop, show the values the line carries that Desktop does not take, naming those the hands-on check finds uncarried. Covers both the moment of choosing and the moment of sending, so no path to a Desktop send leaves the person unaware that the line's model, effort, or bypass flag will not apply. Two indicators to build, keep consistent, and test for one fact, the largest UI cost of the told options; the Settings half depends on the selection mechanism a sibling question owns.

The line keeps its values and neither the Settings window nor the button shows anything; when a click sends the action to Claude Desktop, a notice in VS Code names the line's values the Desktop session will not carry, only those the hands-on check finds uncarried. Tells the person once per send, at the exact moment the values are dropped, with no lasting change to any window's or button's layout. The person learns of it only after the session is already opening, too late to choose a terminal variant instead, and it repeats on every send; it rides beside whatever the person sees after the click, which the Desktop send feedback sibling question owns.

open-question.question: The Over-long Desktop prompt decision runs an action in a VS Code terminal, as an ordinary tracked run, when its prompt is past the limit Claude Desktop accepts, while the Desktop selection mechanism decision has a Claude Desktop line open with a word of its own that names no CLI, so the stored line cannot be run in a terminal as it stands. Which command line does the terminal run for that action?

The Desktop selection mechanism decision has a Claude Desktop line open with a word of its own that names no CLI, and does not say what that word is. Which word opens a Claude Desktop line, as the Settings window's line editor shows it, `~/.gurita/variants.json` stores it, and `gurita-vscode/USAGE.md` documents it?
open-question.alternative: A Claude Desktop line opens with the plain, unqualified word `desktop` (for example `desktop "/gurita:discuss-open-question …" # interactive`), the fourth entry of the command-word list in `src/lineValues.ts` beside `claude`, `agy`, and `codex`, shown so in the line editor, stored so in `~/.gurita/variants.json`, and documented so in `gurita-vscode/USAGE.md`. It is the shortest word and reads like the other three short command words in the line editor; `harnessOf` matches the first word by exact equality, so it needs no parsing change, and no command of that name is on this machine's PATH. It does not say whose desktop: Codex and Antigravity have desktop applications too, so the stored line and USAGE.md need the harness name beside it to be read, and a plain generic word is the likeliest to name some command on another person's PATH, which matters wherever a stored Desktop line is ever run in a terminal as it stands (the Over-long fallback line question owns what the terminal runs).

A Claude Desktop line opens with the plain product-qualified word `claude-desktop`, the fourth entry of the command-word list, shown, stored, and documented so. It names the harness unambiguously in every place the line appears, in the product's own name, so a line in `variants.json` or USAGE.md says which application it opens with no other text, and exact-equality matching keeps it apart from `claude` (no prefix test on `claude` stands in the extension's sources or `runner.py`). It shares the `claude` prefix, so a person scanning lines, or any later prefix test, can take it for a Claude Code line; it is the longest plain word, and as a plain hyphenated word it could still come to name a real command on someone's PATH where a stored line is run in a terminal as it stands.

A Claude Desktop line opens with the generic word marked by a sigil that no installed command carries, `@desktop`, the fourth entry of the command-word list, shown, stored, and documented so. The sigil shows at a glance that the line is not a shell command and makes a collision with a command on PATH practically impossible, removing the plain generic word's collision risk while staying short. The sigil has no precedent in any line form the extension knows, so USAGE.md must explain it, and the word still does not say whose desktop it is.

A Claude Desktop line opens with the product-qualified word marked by a sigil, `@claude-desktop`, the fourth entry of the command-word list, shown, stored, and documented so. It is both unambiguous about the application and visibly not a shell command, so neither a reader nor a terminal can mistake it for a Claude Code line or a runnable command. It is the longest and most unusual opening word, a sigil syntax with no precedent among the line forms that USAGE.md has to introduce, and it crowds the line editor more than any other option.

A Claude Desktop line opens with the link it is sent through, `claude://code/new`, as its first word (for example `claude://code/new "/gurita:discuss-open-question …" # interactive`), the fourth entry of the command-word list, shown, stored, and documented so. The line states its mechanism exactly, the link the Session opening mechanism decision sends, and a word holding `/` is read by any shell as a path, so it can never resolve to a command on PATH and fails plainly if run. It binds every stored line to one link form: if Claude Desktop changes the link or the extension changes how it opens a session, every `custom N` variant in people's `variants.json` holds a stale word; and it looks like a literal URL with the prompt appended, misleading a reader into thinking the line text is what is opened, when the prompt actually travels in the `q` parameter with its values written in.

No word is decided now: the task that adds the fourth harness entry picks it while implementing, and USAGE.md documents whatever it picked. It spends no decision on a naming detail, letting the word be chosen beside the code that parses and rewrites it. The word is a stored format, written into people's `~/.gurita/variants.json` by every pick of the harness dropdown, so a word chosen ad hoc cannot later be renamed without breaking the custom variants already saved, and the tasks writing the harness lists, `rewriteHarness`, the tests, and USAGE.md would each have to agree on it without a recorded decision to read.

open-question.question: Which conflicting decision stands: "Desktop harness availability" or "Session opening mechanism"? The first offers Claude Desktop only where the extension host runs on macOS in a local window and says that in a local Linux window it is not offered and never selectable for an action. The second passes the `claude://code/new` link to the operating system's opener and names `xdg-open` on Linux beside `open` on macOS, a send from Linux that the first rules out.
open-question.alternative: "Desktop harness availability" stands as written: Claude Desktop is offered only in a local macOS window (`process.platform === 'darwin'`, no `vscode.env.remoteName`), never in a local Linux window or a remote one, with no probe. "Session opening mechanism" is rewritten so that the `claude://code/new` link is passed to `open` alone, as an `execFile` child, with the mention of `xdg-open` on Linux removed; the link, its `folder` and prompt values, and the exclusion of the `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option are unchanged. It matches where Claude Desktop actually ships and where it was found: the only installation known to the mission is `/Applications/Claude.app` on macOS, Anthropic publishes no Linux build of the application, and the Desktop Harnesses row's presence check already reads a macOS bundle path, so no opener branch is written for a platform with nothing to open and no Linux path needs a hands-on check the mission has no machine for. A Linux user running an unofficial Claude Desktop build that registers the `claude` URL scheme cannot send an action to it, even though `xdg-open` would likely reach it; widening later means rewriting the availability rule and adding the opener branch then.

"Session opening mechanism" stands as written, `open` on macOS and `xdg-open` on Linux. "Desktop harness availability" is rewritten so that Claude Desktop is offered wherever the extension host runs in a local window on macOS or Linux (`process.platform` of `darwin` or `linux`, no `vscode.env.remoteName`), still never in a remote window, still a fixed rule read from the window with no probe of the application. Linux users with any build that handles the `claude` scheme get the feature with one extra opener name and one extra platform value, and a Linux machine without such a handler fails at the send call, which the Desktop send feedback decision already reports as one error message carrying the opener's cause. It offers a harness on a platform where no official Claude Desktop exists, so for most Linux users the dropdown shows a choice that can only fail on click; the `xdg-open` path, its exit status when no handler is registered, and the folder the session opens in go unverified by the mission's hands-on check, which runs on macOS.

"Session opening mechanism" stands as written, `open` on macOS and `xdg-open` on Linux. "Desktop harness availability" is rewritten so that Claude Desktop is offered in every local macOS window as now, and in a local Linux window only when the Desktop Harnesses row's presence check finds a registered handler of the `claude` URL scheme there (the desktop entry `xdg-mime` reports as the default for `x-scheme-handler/claude`); in a Linux window where none is found, and in every remote window, it is not offered. The rule stays fixed on macOS and gains a probe on Linux only. Linux users who have a build handling the scheme can send, while every other Linux user sees no Desktop choice at all rather than one that fails on click, and the probe reuses the registered-handler test the Harnesses row already makes rather than adding a new kind of check. It reverses the availability entry's no-probe rule and ties selectability to the presence check, which the Desktop Harnesses row decision keeps as information drawn on the row only, so that row's role and its tests grow a gating branch for Linux; the Linux probe and opener path stay unverified by a hands-on check run on macOS.
